claim: An estimated 241 million malaria cases and 627,000 malaria deaths worldwide were reported in 2020.
source: An estimated 241 million malaria cases and 627,000 malaria deaths worldwide were reported in 2020 (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report

claim: World malaria incidence declined by 27% during the first 15 years of this century.
source: Whereas world malaria incidence has declined by 27% during the first 15 years of this century, in the last 4 years it declined by less than 2%, indicating that current interventions to control this deadly disease are waning (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report

claim: In the last 4 years, malaria incidence declined by less than 2%.
source: Whereas world malaria incidence has declined by 27% during the first 15 years of this century, in the last 4 years it declined by less than 2%, indicating that current interventions to control this deadly disease are waning (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report

claim: Current interventions to control malaria are waning.
source: Whereas world malaria incidence has declined by 27% during the first 15 years of this century, in the last 4 years it declined by less than 2%, indicating that current interventions to control this deadly disease are waning (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Inference drawn from the declining effectiveness of interventions as evidenced by reduced rate of malaria incidence decline, supported by WHO citation

claim: The mosquito is an obligatory vector for parasite transmission.
source: The strategy of targeting the mosquito to fight malaria is based on two premises: (1) the mosquito is an obligatory vector for parasite transmission and (2) strong bottlenecks limit parasite development in the mosquito and during transmission to the mammalian host (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2014 and established scientific knowledge

claim: Strong bottlenecks limit parasite development in the mosquito and during transmission to the mammalian host.
source: The strategy of targeting the mosquito to fight malaria is based on two premises: (1) the mosquito is an obligatory vector for parasite transmission and (2) strong bottlenecks limit parasite development in the mosquito and during transmission to the mammalian host (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2014

claim: Of the large number of gametocytes (~10³) ingested by the mosquito, only a few (single digits) ookinetes succeed in traversing the mosquito gut and differentiate into oocysts.
source: Of the large number of gametocytes (~103) ingested by the mosquito, only a few (single digits) ookinetes succeed in traversing the mosquito gut and differentiate into oocysts, defining the first strong bottleneck (Wang and Jacobs-Lorena, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Jacobs-Lorena, 2013

claim: Only a small number of sporozoites (on the order of 1% of total salivary gland content) are delivered when an infected mosquito bites a new individual.
source: Only a small number of these sporozoites (on the order of 1% of total salivary gland content) are delivered when an infected mosquito bites a new individual, defining a second strong bottleneck (Vanderberg, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vanderberg, 1977

claim: Mosquitoes can be engineered to be refractory to the parasite.
source: Since the early demonstration that mosquitoes can be engineered to be refractory to the parasite (Ito et al., 2002), the effectiveness of this approach has been robustly demonstrated in the laboratory by simultaneous expression of multiple effector genes (genes that stop parasite development without affecting the mosquito vector) (Wang et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2020

claim: The effectiveness of engineering mosquitoes to be refractory to parasites has been robustly demonstrated in the laboratory by simultaneous expression of multiple effector genes.
source: Since the early demonstration that mosquitoes can be engineered to be refractory to the parasite (Ito et al., 2002), the effectiveness of this approach has been robustly demonstrated in the laboratory by simultaneous expression of multiple effector genes (genes that stop parasite development without affecting the mosquito vector) (Wang et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2020

claim: Effector genes are genes that stop parasite development without affecting the mosquito vector.
source: Since the early demonstration that mosquitoes can be engineered to be refractory to the parasite (Ito et al., 2002), the effectiveness of this approach has been robustly demonstrated in the laboratory by simultaneous expression of multiple effector genes (genes that stop parasite development without affecting the mosquito vector) (Wang et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Definition provided in the text with supporting citations

claim: Introduction of genes that confer refractoriness into mosquito populations will most likely be achieved by use of CRISPR/Cas9 gene drives.
source: This will most likely be achieved by use of CRISPR/Cas9 gene drives (Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020; Quinn and Nolan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020; Quinn and Nolan, 2020

claim: Paratransgenesis has the advantage that the bacteria occur in the mosquito gut in large numbers, in close proximity to the most vulnerable parasite forms.
source: Paratransgenesis has the advantage that the bacteria occur in the mosquito gut in large numbers, in close proximity to the most vulnerable parasite forms.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about bacterial colonization and parasite development in mosquito gut

claim: Paratransgenesis has been demonstrated to be effective in containing the spread of Trypanosoma cruzi by the Rhodnius prolixus vector.
source: Since the early demonstration of the effectiveness of paratransgenesis to contain the spread of Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease, by the Rhodnius prolixus vector (Durvasula et al., 1997), this approach has been developed for suppressing the mosquito's ability to vector the malaria parasite (Wang et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 1999; Shane et al., 2018; Riehle et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Durvasula et al., 1997

claim: Paratransgenesis has been developed for suppressing the mosquito's ability to vector the malaria parasite.
source: Since the early demonstration of the effectiveness of paratransgenesis to contain the spread of Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease, by the Rhodnius prolixus vector (Durvasula et al., 1997), this approach has been developed for suppressing the mosquito's ability to vector the malaria parasite (Wang et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 1999; Shane et al., 2018; Riehle et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 1999; Shane et al., 2018; Riehle et al., 2007

claim: The mosquito symbiont Serratia AS1 can spread through mosquito populations.
source: As is the case for gene drive, the mosquito symbiont Serratia AS1 can spread through mosquito populations and be engineered to secrete effector proteins (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017

claim: Serratia AS1 can be engineered to secrete effector proteins.
source: As is the case for gene drive, the mosquito symbiont Serratia AS1 can spread through mosquito populations and be engineered to secrete effector proteins (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017

claim: The Q-system was used to constitutively and robustly express antimalaria effector proteins in the midgut and salivary glands of An. stephensi mosquitoes.
source: To constitutively and robustly express antimalaria effector proteins in the midgut and salivary glands of An. stephensi mosquitoes, we used the QF-QUAS binary expression system previously adapted for expression in Anopheles gambiae (Potter et al., 2010b; Riabinina et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Potter et al., 2010b; Riabinina et al., 2016 and described in methods

claim: Two driver mosquito lines were constructed that express the QF transcription factor, one driven by the constitutive salivary gland-specific AAPP promoter and the other driven by the constitutive midgut-specific peritrophin 1 (Aper1) promoter.
source: We constructed two 'driver' mosquito lines that express the QF transcription factor, one driven by the constitutive salivary gland-specific anopheline antiplatelet protein (AAPP) promoter (Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998) and the other driven by the constitutive midgut-specific peritrophin 1 (Aper1) promoter (Abraham et al., 2005; Yoshida and Watanabe, 2006; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998; Abraham et al., 2005; Yoshida and Watanabe, 2006 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: An effector mosquito line was constructed that encodes two parasite inhibiting factors (MP2 and scorpine) downstream of the QUAS promoter and driven by the QF transcription factor.
source: We also constructed a third 'effector' mosquito line that encodes two parasite inhibiting factors (MP2 and scorpine) downstream of the QUAS promoter and driven by the QF transcription factor (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The midgut peptide 2 (MP2) dodecapeptide binds tightly to the mosquito midgut epithelium and inhibits Plasmodium falciparum invasion with high efficiency.
source: The midgut peptide 2 (MP2) dodecapeptide, identified from a phage display screen, binds tightly to the mosquito midgut epithelium, and inhibits Plasmodium falciparum invasion with high efficiency (Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014), whereas the scorpion (Pandinus imperator) peptide scorpine lyses malaria parasites without affecting mosquito fitness (Conde et al., 2000; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014

claim: The scorpion peptide scorpine lyses malaria parasites without affecting mosquito fitness.
source: The midgut peptide 2 (MP2) dodecapeptide, identified from a phage display screen, binds tightly to the mosquito midgut epithelium, and inhibits Plasmodium falciparum invasion with high efficiency (Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014), whereas the scorpion (Pandinus imperator) peptide scorpine lyses malaria parasites without affecting mosquito fitness (Conde et al., 2000; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Conde et al., 2000; Gao et al., 2010

claim: Two midgut driver lines (Mg1 and Mg2), two salivary gland driver lines (Sg1 and Sg2), and two effector lines (E1 and E2) were obtained.
source: Two midgut driver lines (Mg1 and Mg2), two salivary gland driver lines (Sg1 and Sg2), and two effector lines (E1 and E2) were obtained.
evidence: Described in results section

claim: All the parental lines, except for Sg2, have insertions in intergenic regions.
source: All the parental lines, except for Sg2, have insertions in intergenic regions.
evidence: Based on splinkerette PCR and sequencing data presented in Appendix 1—table 1

claim: Two of the three Sg2 insertions are in intergenic regions, and one in the open-reading frame of the gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase gene (ASTE010947).
source: Two of the three Sg2 insertions are in intergenic regions, and one in the open-reading frame of the gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase gene (ASTE010947).
evidence: Based on splinkerette PCR and sequencing data

claim: After the 10th generation, 100% of offspring from transgenic lines showed the same fluorescence as the parent females, consistent with all transgenic lines being homozygous.
source: After the 10th generation, 20 transgenic female mosquitoes from each line were mated with wild-type (WT) males, and 100% the offspring showed the same fluorescence as the parent females, consistent with all transgenic lines being homozygous (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in Appendix 1—table 2

claim: In the midgut, the scorpine transcript was between 44-fold and 56-fold higher than that of the endogenous Aper mRNA.
source: In the midgut, the scorpine transcript was between 44- (p<0.01) and 56-fold (p<0.01) higher than that of the endogenous Aper mRNA and the MP2 transcript abundance was between 49- (p<0.001) and 36-fold (p<0.01) higher, depending on the transgenic line (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C and Appendix 1—table 3

claim: In the midgut, the MP2 transcript abundance was between 49-fold and 36-fold higher than that of the endogenous Aper mRNA.
source: In the midgut, the scorpine transcript was between 44- (p<0.01) and 56-fold (p<0.01) higher than that of the endogenous Aper mRNA and the MP2 transcript abundance was between 49- (p<0.001) and 36-fold (p<0.01) higher, depending on the transgenic line (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C and Appendix 1—table 3

claim: In the salivary glands, scorpine transcript abundance varied between 27-fold and 63-fold higher than that of the endogenous AAPP mRNA.
source: In the salivary glands, scorpine transcript abundance varied between 27- (p<0.05) and 63-fold (p<0.01) higher and MP2 transcript between 49- (p<0.001) and 140-fold (p<0.01) higher than that of the endogenous AAPP mRNA, depending on the transgenic line (Figure 1D, Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D and Appendix 1—table 4

claim: In the salivary glands, MP2 transcript abundance varied between 49-fold and 140-fold higher than that of the endogenous AAPP mRNA.
source: In the salivary glands, scorpine transcript abundance varied between 27- (p<0.05) and 63-fold (p<0.01) higher and MP2 transcript between 49- (p<0.001) and 140-fold (p<0.01) higher than that of the endogenous AAPP mRNA, depending on the transgenic line (Figure 1D, Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D and Appendix 1—table 4

claim: In the absence of a driver, transgene expression in 'E' effector mosquitoes was undetectable.
source: Moreover, in the absence of a driver, transgene expression in 'E' effector mosquitoes (see Figure 1A) was undetectable (Appendix 1—table 3 and Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data presented in Appendix 1—table 3 and Appendix 1—table 4

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed the tissue-specific expression of the MP2 (6.17 kDa) and scorpine (8.46 kDa) proteins.
source: Western blot analysis using anti-MP2 and anti-scorpine antibodies confirmed the tissue-specific expression of the MP2 (6.17 kDa) and scorpine (8.46 kDa) proteins (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F

claim: No significant longevity differences were detected for any female or male transgenic mosquitoes compared to wild-type.
source: No significant longevity differences were detected for any female (Appendix 1—figure 2A) or male (Appendix 1—figure 2B) transgenic mosquitoes compared to WT.
evidence: Based on survival data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2A and 2B

claim: Mosquitoes from all parental and antimalaria-expressing transgenic lines showed no difference in fecundity when compared to wild-type mosquitoes.
source: Mosquitoes from all parental and antimalaria-expressing transgenic lines showed no difference in fecundity when compared to WT mosquitoes (Appendix 1—figure 2C).
evidence: Based on fecundity data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2C

claim: No significant differences in fertility were detected for the Mg and Sg/E lines when compared to wild-type.
source: As for fertility, no significant differences were detected for the Mg and Sg/E lines when compared to WT, while only marginal differences were detected for the Sg, E, Mg/E, and Mg/Sg/E lines (2.0, 3.1, 2.0, and 2.0% reduction, respectively) (Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: Based on fertility data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2D

claim: Only marginal differences in fertility were detected for the Sg, E, Mg/E, and Mg/Sg/E lines (2.0, 3.1, 2.0, and 2.0% reduction, respectively).
source: As for fertility, no significant differences were detected for the Mg and Sg/E lines when compared to WT, while only marginal differences were detected for the Sg, E, Mg/E, and Mg/Sg/E lines (2.0, 3.1, 2.0, and 2.0% reduction, respectively) (Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: Based on fertility data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2D

claim: Neither transgenesis nor antimalaria gene expression affects blood ingestion.
source: We found no significant differences (Appendix 1—figure 2E and F), suggesting that neither transgenesis nor antimalaria gene expression affects blood ingestion.
evidence: Based on blood feeding data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2E and F

claim: There are no differences in lifespan, fertility, or fecundity among wild-type, transgenic, and (transgenic plus paratransgenic) mosquitoes.
source: In further experiments, we found that there are no differences in lifespan, fertility, or fecundity among WT, transgenic, and (transgenic plus paratransgenic) mosquitoes (Appendix 1—figure 3A–D).
evidence: Based on fitness data presented in Appendix 1—figure 3A–D

claim: Transgenesis, antimalaria gene expression in the midgut and/or salivary glands, and paratransgenesis do not impair mosquito survival, fecundity, fertility, and blood feeding under laboratory conditions.
source: In summary, our data show that transgenesis, antimalaria gene expression in the midgut and/or salivary glands, and paratransgenesis do not impair mosquito survival, fecundity, fertility (only minor differences), and blood feeding under laboratory conditions.
evidence: Summary of fitness data from multiple experiments

claim: Serratia AS1-multi equally populate wild-type and transgenic mosquito midguts, ovaries, and accessory glands.
source: We found that Serratia AS1-multi equally populate WT and transgenic mosquito midguts, ovaries, and accessory glands and are transmitted for at least three generations (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Based on bacterial colonization data shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: Serratia AS1-multi are transmitted for at least three generations.
source: We found that Serratia AS1-multi equally populate WT and transgenic mosquito midguts, ovaries, and accessory glands and are transmitted for at least three generations (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Based on vertical transmission data shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: Wild-type and transgenic male mosquitoes colonized with Serratia AS1-multi transferred the bacteria horizontally (sexually) to virgin wild-type and transgenic female mosquitoes.
source: Moreover, we found that WT and transgenic male mosquitoes colonized with Serratia AS1-multi transferred the bacteria horizontally (sexually) to virgin WT and transgenic female mosquitoes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on horizontal transmission data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Horizontal transfer of Serratia did not take place when male mosquitoes were placed with mated females, showing that transfer occurs during copulation.
source: Horizontal transfer did not take place when male mosquitoes were placed with mated females, showing that transfer occurs during copulation (Appendix 1—table 5; female mosquitoes mate only once in their lifetime).
evidence: Based on experimental data in Appendix 1—table 5 and established knowledge about mosquito mating behavior

claim: Recombinant Serratia AS1 can effectively populate transgenic mosquitoes and be transmitted through multiple generations.
source: These results suggest that recombinant Serratia AS1 can effectively populate transgenic mosquitoes and be transmitted through multiple generations.
evidence: Inference drawn from the colonization and transmission data

claim: Mosquitoes cannot inoculate Serratia bacteria while feeding on a host.
source: Experiments seeking evidence for possible bacteria transmission with a mosquito bite yielded negative results (Appendix 1—figure 4), suggesting that mosquitoes cannot inoculate the bacteria while feeding on a host.
evidence: Based on experimental data in Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: Expression of effector molecules in the midgut or in the salivary glands of transgenic mosquitoes significantly reduced parasite burden.
source: As shown in Figure 3, expression of effector molecules in the midgut or in the salivary glands of transgenic mosquitoes significantly reduced parasite burden, whereas concomitant effector expression in both organs reduced burden to the greatest extent (81.0 and 85.2% inhibition of mean oocyst and sporozoite numbers, respectively).
evidence: Based on parasite burden data shown in Figure 3

claim: Concomitant effector expression in both midgut and salivary glands reduced parasite burden to the greatest extent (81.0 and 85.2% inhibition of mean oocyst and sporozoite numbers, respectively).
source: As shown in Figure 3, expression of effector molecules in the midgut or in the salivary glands of transgenic mosquitoes significantly reduced parasite burden, whereas concomitant effector expression in both organs reduced burden to the greatest extent (81.0 and 85.2% inhibition of mean oocyst and sporozoite numbers, respectively).
evidence: Based on parasite burden data shown in Figure 3

claim: Effector-expressing recombinant bacteria significantly reduced parasite burden in wild-type mosquitoes (69.6 and 65.4% inhibition of oocyst and sporozoite numbers, respectively).
source: Effector-expressing recombinant bacteria also significantly reduced parasite burden in WT mosquitoes (69.6 and 65.4% inhibition of oocyst and sporozoite numbers, respectively).
evidence: Based on parasite burden data from paratransgenic experiments

claim: Wild-type bacteria also inhibited to some extent oocyst formation in wild-type mosquitoes.
source: As found previously (Wang et al., 2017), WT bacteria also inhibited to some extent oocyst formation in WT mosquitoes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017 and data from current study

claim: Combining mosquito transgenesis with paratransgenesis led to the strongest inhibition of parasite development.
source: Importantly, combining mosquito transgenesis with paratransgenesis led to the strongest inhibition of parasite development.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of parasite burden data

claim: Oocyst prevalence was reduced from 98.0% to 49.0% for transgenic-only mosquitoes and to 47.8% when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
source: Oocyst prevalence was reduced from 98.0% to 49.0% for transgenic-only mosquitoes and to 47.8% when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
evidence: Based on oocyst prevalence data from infection experiments

claim: Sporozoite prevalence was reduced from 97.4% to 42.4% for transgenic-only mosquitoes and to 24.1% when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
source: Sporozoite prevalence was reduced from 97.4% to 42.4% for transgenic-only mosquitoes and to 24.1% when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
evidence: Based on sporozoite prevalence data from infection experiments

claim: For all transgenic and paratransgenic combinations, ookinete formation was strongly inhibited.
source: For all transgenic and paratransgenic combinations, ookinete formation was strongly inhibited, suggesting that the effector molecules affect the early parasite stages in the mosquito midgut.
evidence: Based on ookinete formation data in Appendix 1—figure 5

claim: The effector molecules affect the early parasite stages in the mosquito midgut.
source: For all transgenic and paratransgenic combinations, ookinete formation was strongly inhibited, suggesting that the effector molecules affect the early parasite stages in the mosquito midgut.
evidence: Inference drawn from ookinete inhibition data

claim: When mice were challenged with the bite of three wild-type mosquitoes, 100% became infected (half-infection time = 5.5 ± 0.5 days).
source: When mice were challenged with the bite of three WT mosquitoes (three independent experiments with five mice each), 100% became infected (half-infection time = 5.5 ± 0.5 days) (Figure 4B) and their salivary glands had a median 8400 sporozoites (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on transmission data shown in Figure 4B and 4C

claim: With paratransgenic mosquitoes (three mosquito bites), 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time 7.1 ± 0.7 days), and their salivary glands had a median of 2100 sporozoites (74% lower than wild-type mosquitoes).
source: With mosquitoes carrying Serratia AS1-multi (paratransgenic), 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time 7.1 ± 0.7 days), and their salivary glands had a median of 2100 sporozoites (74% lower than WT mosquitoes).
evidence: Based on transmission data from paratransgenic mosquito experiments

claim: With transgenic mosquitoes (three mosquito bites), 67% of the mice were not infected, and their salivary glands had a median of 900 sporozoites (92% lower than wild-type mosquitoes).
source: With transgenic mosquitoes, 67% of the mice were not infected, and their salivary glands had a median of 900 sporozoites (92% lower than WT mosquitoes).
evidence: Based on transmission data from transgenic mosquito experiments

claim: With (paratransgenic + transgenic) mosquitoes (three mosquito bites), 93% mice were not infected, and their salivary glands had a median of zero sporozoites (100% lower than wild-type mosquitoes).
source: With (paratransgenic + transgenic) mosquitoes, 93% mice were not infected, and their salivary glands had a median of zero sporozoites (100% lower than WT mosquitoes).
evidence: Based on transmission data from combined transgenic and paratransgenic mosquito experiments

claim: When mice were challenged with the bite of five wild-type mosquitoes, only 1 mouse out of 15 (6.7%) did not get infected (half-infection time = 5.6 ± 0.7 days).
source: When mice were challenged with the bite of five WT mosquitoes (Figure 4D and E), only 1 mouse out of 15 (6.7%) did not get infected (half-infection time = 5.6 ± 0.7 days).
evidence: Based on transmission data shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: With paratransgenesis (five mosquito bites), 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 8.3 ± 1.0).
source: With paratransgenesis, 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 8.3 ± 1.0), with transgenesis 47% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 10.1 ± 1.0 days) and with (paratransgenesis + transgenesis) 80% of the mice were not infected.
evidence: Based on transmission data from five mosquito bite experiments

claim: With transgenesis (five mosquito bites), 47% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 10.1 ± 1.0 days).
source: With paratransgenesis, 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 8.3 ± 1.0), with transgenesis 47% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 10.1 ± 1.0 days) and with (paratransgenesis + transgenesis) 80% of the mice were not infected.
evidence: Based on transmission data from five mosquito bite experiments

claim: With (paratransgenesis + transgenesis) (five mosquito bites), 80% of the mice were not infected.
source: With paratransgenesis, 26.7% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 8.3 ± 1.0), with transgenesis 47% of the mice were not infected (half-infection time = 10.1 ± 1.0 days) and with (paratransgenesis + transgenesis) 80% of the mice were not infected.
evidence: Based on transmission data from five mosquito bite experiments

claim: Transgenic and paratransgenic expression of effector molecules are both effective in impairing transmission, but the combination of the two strategies is considerably more effective.
source: In summary, our data shows that transgenic and paratransgenic expression of effector molecules are both effective in impairing transmission, but that the combination of the two strategies is considerably more effective.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on transmission data

claim: Effector mRNA abundance was about 50 times higher than that of the endogenous genes.
source: Notably, effector mRNA abundance was about 50 times higher than that of the endogenous genes, consistent with the high effectiveness of the Q-system in Drosophila (Potter et al., 2010b).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data and supported by citation to Potter et al., 2010b

claim: Some QF toxicity was reported when the Q-system was first used in Drosophila.
source: Some QF toxicity was reported when the Q-system was first used in Drosophila (Potter et al., 2010b; Riabinina et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Potter et al., 2010b; Riabinina et al., 2016

claim: Expression of neither the QF transcription factor nor the antimalaria effectors affected mosquito longevity, blood meal uptake, or offspring production under laboratory conditions.
source: Of note, expression of neither the QF transcription factor nor the antimalaria effectors affected mosquito longevity, blood meal uptake, or offspring production under laboratory conditions.
evidence: Based on fitness data from multiple experiments

claim: MP2 is a 12-amino-acid peptide that likely targets a midgut receptor for ookinete traversal.
source: MP2 is a 12-amino-acid peptide that likely targets a midgut receptor for ookinete traversal (Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014), and scorpine is an antimicrobial toxin hybrid between a cecropin and a defensin that lyses Plasmodium ookinetes (Conde et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014

claim: Scorpine is an antimicrobial toxin hybrid between a cecropin and a defensin that lyses Plasmodium ookinetes.
source: MP2 is a 12-amino-acid peptide that likely targets a midgut receptor for ookinete traversal (Vega-Rodríguez et al., 2014), and scorpine is an antimicrobial toxin hybrid between a cecropin and a defensin that lyses Plasmodium ookinetes (Conde et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conde et al., 2000

claim: Scorpine expressed by the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium in the mosquito hemocoel strongly inhibits (~90%) salivary gland sporozoite numbers.
source: Scorpine expressed by the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium in the mosquito hemocoel strongly inhibits (~90%) salivary gland sporozoite numbers (Fang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fang et al., 2011

claim: Transgenic mosquitoes expressing scorpine in the salivary glands were highly effective in reducing sporozoite numbers.
source: Transgenic mosquitoes expressing this effector in the salivary glands were also highly effective in reducing sporozoite numbers (this work).
evidence: Based on data from current study

claim: Expression of both effector genes in the midgut and the salivary glands led to a much stronger decrease of salivary gland sporozoite numbers than the expression of the effectors in either of these organs alone.
source: Furthermore, expression of both effector genes in the midgut and the salivary glands led to a much stronger decrease of salivary gland sporozoite numbers than the expression of the effectors in either of these organs alone.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of sporozoite data

claim: Expression of antimalaria effectors in the salivary glands inhibited oocyst development in the midgut.
source: That expression of antimalaria effectors in the salivary glands inhibited oocyst development in the midgut (Sg/E; Figure 3A) is most likely explained by the fact that mosquitoes ingest saliva with the blood meal, in this way incorporating effector proteins into the blood bolus (Luo et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on oocyst data in Figure 3A and supported by citation to Luo et al., 2000

claim: Mosquitoes ingest saliva with the blood meal, incorporating effector proteins into the blood bolus.
source: That expression of antimalaria effectors in the salivary glands inhibited oocyst development in the midgut (Sg/E; Figure 3A) is most likely explained by the fact that mosquitoes ingest saliva with the blood meal, in this way incorporating effector proteins into the blood bolus (Luo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2000

claim: Human PAI-1 expressed in salivary glands was ingested together with the saliva and inhibited oocyst formation.
source: A similar phenomenon was also observed in a recent report showing that human PAI-1 expressed in salivary glands was ingested together with the saliva and inhibited oocyst formation (Pascini et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pascini et al., 2022

claim: The multi-effector protein, in addition to the AAPP salivary gland protein, was present in the midguts of Sg/E mosquitoes that express the multi-effector protein only in the salivary glands.
source: In our study, we confirmed the presence of the multi-effector protein, in addition to the AAPP salivary gland protein (control), in the midguts of Sg/E mosquitoes that express the multi-effector protein only in the salivary glands (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: Based on Western blot data in Appendix 1—figure 7

claim: Scorpine has been shown to be nontoxic to insect cells.
source: Scorpine has been shown to be nontoxic to insect cells (Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2008), whereas MP2 toxicity was not determined previously.
evidence: Supported by citation to Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2008

claim: MP2 toxicity was not determined previously.
source: Scorpine has been shown to be nontoxic to insect cells (Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2008), whereas MP2 toxicity was not determined previously.
evidence: Statement about lack of prior data

claim: Mosquitoes cannot inoculate Serratia bacteria while feeding on a host.
source: Experiments seeking evidence for possible bacteria transmission with a mosquito bite yielded negative results (Appendix 1—figure 4), suggesting that mosquitoes cannot inoculate the bacteria while feeding on a host.
evidence: Based on experimental data in Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: Secretion of effector proteins by recombinant Pantoea, Serratia, or Asaia bacteria into the midgut inhibits Plasmodium development.
source: It was previously shown that secretion of effector proteins by recombinant Pantoea (Wang et al., 2012), Serratia (Wang et al., 2017), or Asaia (Shane et al., 2018) bacteria into the midgut inhibits Plasmodium development and that WT Serratia AS1 is transmitted from one mosquito generation to the next (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017; Shane et al., 2018

claim: Wild-type Serratia AS1 is transmitted from one mosquito generation to the next.
source: It was previously shown that secretion of effector proteins by recombinant Pantoea (Wang et al., 2012), Serratia (Wang et al., 2017), or Asaia (Shane et al., 2018) bacteria into the midgut inhibits Plasmodium development and that WT Serratia AS1 is transmitted from one mosquito generation to the next (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017

claim: The engineered Serratia were efficiently transmitted from one mosquito generation to the next.
source: Our experiments showed that the engineered Serratia were efficiently transmitted from one mosquito generation to the next, a result that bodes well for the implementation of the paratransgenesis strategy in the field.
evidence: Based on vertical transmission data from current study

claim: The combination of transgenesis and paratransgenesis greatly reduced parasite development in the mosquito.
source: The combination of transgenesis and paratransgenesis greatly reduced parasite development in the mosquito, and most importantly, it resulted in a high-level reduction of transmission from an infected to a naïve mouse compared to the individual interventions.
evidence: Based on parasite development and transmission data

claim: The combination of transgenesis and paratransgenesis resulted in a high-level reduction of transmission from an infected to a naïve mouse compared to the individual interventions.
source: The combination of transgenesis and paratransgenesis greatly reduced parasite development in the mosquito, and most importantly, it resulted in a high-level reduction of transmission from an infected to a naïve mouse compared to the individual interventions.
evidence: Based on transmission data from mouse challenge experiments

claim: When naïve mice were bitten by three (transgenic + paratransgenic) mosquitoes, 93% of the mice (14 out of 15) did not develop an infection compared with 100% infection when mice were bitten by wild-type mosquitoes.
source: When naïve mice were bitten by three (transgenic + paratransgenic) mosquitoes, 93% of the mice (14 out of 15) did not develop an infection compared with 100% infection when mice were bitten by WT mosquitoes.
evidence: Based on transmission data from three mosquito bite experiments

claim: In the field, where the density of infected mosquitoes is low even in high-transmission areas, it is unlikely that people will be consecutively bitten by more than one infected mosquito.
source: In the field, where the density of infected mosquitoes is low even in high-transmission areas, it is unlikely that people will be consecutively bitten by more than one infected mosquito, and protection from transmission is expected to be very high.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about mosquito density in field conditions

claim: Protection from transmission is expected to be very high in field conditions.
source: In the field, where the density of infected mosquitoes is low even in high-transmission areas, it is unlikely that people will be consecutively bitten by more than one infected mosquito, and protection from transmission is expected to be very high.
evidence: Inference based on laboratory data and field conditions

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology has afforded the development of promising gene drive systems focused on population suppression or population modification strategies.
source: In this respect, CRISPR/Cas9 technology has afforded the development of promising gene drive systems focused on population suppression or population modification strategies (Scudellari, 2019; Nolan, 2021; Simoni et al., 2020; Adolfi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scudellari, 2019; Nolan, 2021; Simoni et al., 2020; Adolfi et al., 2020

claim: Population reduction leaves an empty biological niche that upon cessation of reduction pressure will result in recolonization by the same or other mosquito species.
source: Population reduction leaves an empty biological niche that upon cessation of reduction pressure will result in recolonization by the same or other mosquito species.
evidence: Based on ecological principles and inference

claim: Population modification results in a more stable state, with a biological niche occupied by mosquitoes that are poor transmitters.
source: In contrast, population modification results in a more stable state, with a biological niche occupied by mosquitoes that are poor transmitters.
evidence: Based on ecological principles and inference

claim: Efficient spread of recombinant bacteria into mosquito populations has been demonstrated in a laboratory setting.
source: Similarly, efficient spread of recombinant bacteria into mosquito populations has been demonstrated in a laboratory setting (reference Wang et al., 2017 and this work), indicating a promising path toward the field implementation of the most efficient (transgenesis + paratransgenesis) strategy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017 and data from current study

claim: A naturally occurring and nonmodified Serratia can spread through mosquito populations while strongly suppressing Plasmodium development.
source: The recent finding that a naturally occurring and nonmodified Serratia can spread through mosquito populations while strongly suppressing Plasmodium development (Gao et al., 2021) significantly increases the feasibility of moving a paratransgenesis-like approach into the field as it bypasses concerns relating to the release of genetically modified organisms in nature.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2021

claim: Transgenesis and paratransgenesis are compatible with current vector and malaria control measures such as insecticide-based mosquito control, mass drug administration, and vaccines.
source: Notably, transgenesis and paratransgenesis are not envisioned to be implemented by themselves. Both are compatible with current vector and malaria control measures such as insecticide-based mosquito control, mass drug administration, and vaccines, and their added implementation promises to substantially enhance the effectiveness of intervention of disease transmission.
evidence: Based on inference about compatibility of different intervention strategies

claim: The Q-binary system to express anti-Plasmodium effectors in the mosquito is highly efficient.
source: In summary, we show that the Q-binary system to express anti-Plasmodium effectors in the mosquito is highly efficient.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on expression data

claim: Recombinant Serratia AS1 is horizontally and vertically transmitted across multiple mosquito generations.
source: We also show that in addition to inhibiting parasite development, recombinant Serratia AS1 is horizontally and vertically transmitted across multiple mosquito generations, which is a bacteria counterpart of gene drive.
evidence: Based on transmission data from current study

claim: The combination of transgenesis with paratransgenesis provides maximum parasite blocking activity and has high potential for fighting malaria.
source: A major conclusion of this work is that the combination of transgenesis with paratransgenesis provides maximum parasite blocking activity and has high potential for fighting malaria.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data

claim: Both mosquito-based and bacteria-based approaches strongly reduced the oocyst and sporozoite intensity.
source: Whereas both mosquito-based and bacteria-based approaches strongly reduced the oocyst and sporozoite intensity, a substantially stronger reduction of Plasmodium falciparum development was achieved when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
evidence: Based on parasite burden data from P. falciparum experiments

claim: A substantially stronger reduction of Plasmodium falciparum development was achieved when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
source: Whereas both mosquito-based and bacteria-based approaches strongly reduced the oocyst and sporozoite intensity, a substantially stronger reduction of Plasmodium falciparum development was achieved when transgenesis and paratransgenesis were combined.
evidence: Based on comparative parasite burden data

claim: Transmission of Plasmodium berghei from infected to naïve mice was maximally inhibited by the combination of transgenesis and paratransgenesis.
source: Most importantly, transmission of Plasmodium berghei from infected to naïve mice was maximally inhibited by the combination of the two approaches.
evidence: Based on transmission data from P. berghei experiments

claim: Combining transgenesis and paratransgenesis promises to become a powerful approach to combat malaria.
source: Combining these two strategies promises to become a powerful approach to combat malaria.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data and future potential
